title-group.article-title: Trampoline exercise reduces anxiety and improves motor skills in children with autism spectrum disorder: A randomized controlled trial

sec.title: Background:
sec.p: Anxiety affects approximately 40% to 50% of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet evidence-based nonpharmacological interventions remain limited. Trampoline exercise, which combines vestibular stimulation and aerobic activity, may offer dual benefits by reducing anxiety and improving motor skills in this population. To examine the effects of an 8-week trampoline exercise program on anxiety, motor performance, and physiological outcomes (heart rate variability, HRV) in children with mild-to-moderate ASD.

sec.title: Methods:
sec.p: This assessor-blinded, randomized controlled trial (Registered at Chinese Clinical Trial Registry: ChiCTR2500104402; Date: June 17, 2025) enrolled 50 children with mild-to-moderate ASD (aged 9–14 years) from Shandong Special Education Rehabilitation Center, China. Participants were allocated 1:1 to an 8-week trampoline intervention group (IG, n = 25; 3 sessions/wk, 30 min/session) or a resistance training control group (CG, n = 25). Primary outcomes: anxiety (screen for child anxiety related disorders [SCARED] questionnaire) and HRV root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD). Secondary outcomes: standing long jump (SLJ), one-leg stance with eyes closed (OLS), and BMI (body mass index). Between-group differences were analyzed via Mann–Whitney U tests; effect sizes were reported as Cliff δ (thresholds: small = 0.11, medium = 0.28, large = 0.43).

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: All 50 participants completed the intervention and assessments. Compared with CG, IG showed significantly greater reductions in SCARED scores (Δ = −9.4 vs Δ = 0, false discovery rate-corrected P < .001, δ = −0.92) and improvements in HRV (RMSSD: Δ = +8.51 ms vs Δ = +1.45 ms, false discovery rate-corrected P = .003, δ = −0.66). Standing long jump (SLJ) improved markedly in IG (Δ = +15.0 cm vs CG Δ = +4.0 cm, false discovery rate-corrected P < .001, δ = −0.68). However, one-leg stance with eyes closed (OLS) showed no significant between-group difference after false discovery rate correction (Δ = +0.65 seconds vs Δ = +1.14 seconds, false discovery rate-corrected P = .076, δ = −0.37). BMI remained stable in both groups (false discovery rate-corrected P = .348).

sec.title: Conclusion:
sec.p: Trampoline exercise significantly reduces anxiety and enhances lower limb explosive power in children with mild-to-moderate ASD, with effect sizes exceeding clinical thresholds. Its low cost (<$100) and high adherence (85%) support integration into school-based interventions. Future studies should explore long-term effects (3–6 months) and neural mechanisms via functional magnetic resonance imaging.
Keywords: anxiety, autism spectrum disorder, heart rate variability, motor skills, trampoline exercise

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental condition defined by persistent challenges in social communication and interaction, paired with restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities.[1] Early identification – marked by indicators such as limited eye contact, delayed responses to one’s name, and language regression – is critical for timely intervention.[2] Beyond its core symptoms, ASD frequently co-occurs with other conditions, including anxiety, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and mood disorders.[2-4]

Children with ASD often exhibit significant motor impairments and poor sensory integration, which contribute to deficits in gross and fine motor skills, atypical gait, and coordination difficulties.[5,6] Additionally, a combination of sedentary lifestyles and abnormal eating behaviors increases their risk of obesity.[7] Anxiety, in particular, is a highly prevalent comorbidity, affecting an estimated 40% to 50% of individuals with ASD[8]; it is also linked to depressive symptoms and self-injurious behaviors.[9] Physiologically, children with ASD commonly display dysregulation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, leading to elevated cortisol levels and greater vulnerability to stress and anxiety.[10] Heart rate variability (HRV) – a noninvasive measure of autonomic nervous system function – has been identified as a reliable physiological marker of anxiety in this group, with lower HRV indicating heightened anxiety.[11,12]

Physical exercise has emerged as a promising non-pharmacological intervention to reduce anxiety and improve physical health in children with ASD. Various forms of exercise – including jogging, aquatic activities, and structured aerobic programs –have shown potential for alleviating anxiety symptoms.[13] Preliminary research suggests that trampoline-based activities may reduce stereotyped behaviors,[14] enhance attention, and promote relaxation and stress reduction[15]; their potential to improve motor skills and balance has also been noted.[16-19] Among these, trampoline exercise has gained attention due to its unique combination of vestibular stimulation and aerobic exertion. Notably, the synergistic effect of rhythmic vestibular input and cardiovascular exercise may simultaneously target both anxiety (via autonomic modulation) and motor deficits – a dual benefit not typically achieved through conventional exercises like jogging or swimming. The repeated stretch-shortening cycles during trampoline jumping resemble plyometric training patterns, which are known to enhance neuromuscular adaptations and explosive strength.[20] Anxiety assessment in children with ASD commonly uses validated standardized scales,[21] and pharmacotherapy remains a conventional intervention for emotional and behavioral symptoms in ASD.[22] Neuromodulation techniques offer a novel intervention approach for autonomic nervous system dysfunction in ASD,[23] and cognitive behavioral therapy has been proven effective in alleviating anxiety in autistic adolescents.[24] The detection and analysis of HRV in this study strictly followed the universal standards in the cardiovascular field.[25] The lack of significant changes in BMI following short-term exercise interventions can be explained by the energy compensation effect,[26] and the evidence-based early intervention system for ASD also provides a framework for the design of school-based intervention programs.[27]

Despite this growing interest, however, existing evidence remains limited and largely preliminary. Many prior studies are small in scale, lack controlled designs, or focus primarily on motor outcomes without rigorously quantifying anxiety using both psychometric tools (e.g., questionnaires) and physiological measures (e.g., HRV). There is a notable shortage of randomized controlled trials specifically examining the anxiolytic effects of structured trampoline exercise in children with ASD,[28] and the mechanisms underlying its potential benefits are not well understood. Furthermore, the prevalence of ASD continues to rise, with recent surveillance data indicating that approximately 1 in 36 children aged 8 years is identified with ASD.[29] The promotion of school-based physical activity is a core public health initiative for improving the health of children with special needs,[30] which further underscores the urgent need to develop scalable, evidence-based nonpharmacological interventions for ASD.[31] To address these gaps, this study aimed to: evaluate the effects of an 8-week structured trampoline exercise program on anxiety (measured via the SCARED questionnaire and HRV) and motor skills (assessed using the standing long jump and single-leg balance tests) in children with mild-to-moderate ASD; assess the feasibility of implementing trampoline exercise in school-based interventions through monitoring of adherence and safety; and explore the relationship between physical activity engagement and anxiety reduction, given emerging evidence linking physical activity to resilient coping in various populations.

sec.title: 2.1. Study design
sec.p: This assessor-blinded, randomized controlled trial employed a 2-arm parallel design to evaluate the effects of an 8-week trampoline exercise intervention on anxiety, motor performance, and physiological outcomes in children with ASD. This study was conducted by the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Center for Ethics in Human Research in Khon Kaen University (No. HE672160) and registration number ChiCTR2500104402 as of June 17, 2025 and it was accessible at https://www.chictr.org.cn/. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained from the parents or legal guardians of all participants prior to enrollment.

sec.title: 2.2. Sample size calculation
sec.p: The sample size was determined from preliminary data from a feasibility study (n = 6 per group), which indicated a standard effect size (Cohen d) of 0.5 and a pooled standard deviation of 1.17. Using a 2-tailed α = 0.05 and G*Power 3.1 for 80% power, a minimum of 13 participants was required for each group. To compensate for the expected 10% dropout rate, the researcher recruited 25 participants per group, resulting in a total sample size of 50 (Fig. 1). Although the sample size estimation relied on a small pilot study, the observed effect sizes in the actual trial were substantial, and post hoc power analysis confirmed adequate statistical power for the primary outcomes.

sec.title: 2.3. Participants
sec.p: We recruited 50 children (aged 9–14 years) diagnosed with mild-to-moderate ASD from the Shandong Special Education Rehabilitation Center, China. The inclusion criteria were as follows: clinical ASD diagnosis (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition criteria); no concurrent musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, or neurological contraindications to exercise; and ability to follow verbal instructions. The exclusion criteria were as follows: comorbid epilepsy or spinal abnormalities; recent fractures/surgery; and uncontrolled asthma.

sec.title: 2.4. Randomization and blinding
sec.p: Participants were stratified by age (9–11 vs 12–14 years) and gender. An independent statistician who was not involved in participant recruitment or outcome assessment generated the random allocation sequence using a computer-based random number generator (block sizes of 6 and 8, randomly varied) via SAS 9.4 software. The allocation sequence was concealed in sequentially numbered, sealed, opaque envelopes. Prior to the intervention, an on-site researcher not involved in outcome assessment opened the envelopes in sequential order to assign participants to either the IG or the CG in a 1:1 ratio. Outcome assessors remained blinded to group assignment throughout the study; however, due to the nature of the intervention, participants and trainers were not blinded.

sec.title: 2.5.1.1. Intervention group (IG)
sec.p: The intervention spanned 8 weeks, with a total of 24 sessions. The participants had 3 sessions per week, each lasting 30 minutes. Every session was structured as follows: Warm-up (5 minutes): light jogging and dynamic stretching were used to prepare the body for the upcoming exercise. Main exercise (20 minutes): Participants engaged in progressive trampoline activities as detailed in Table 1. These activities included rhythmic jumping, balance tasks such as single-leg stands, and goal-directed movements such as touching suspended objects. Cool-down (5 minutes): Comprising deep breathing and gentle stretching to help the body recover and reduce muscle soreness.

sec.title: 2.5.1.2. Control group (CG)
sec.p: The CG participated in an 8-week resistance band training program, which had the same training frequency (3 times a week), training duration (30 minutes each time), and attention level as the IG. Through resistance training, that is, eliminating the key vestibular-aerobic components of the trampoline exercise, we aimed to isolate the specific therapeutic benefits provided by the unique rhythmic vestibular stimulation and aerobic exercise combination offered by the trampoline intervention. The training content included bicep curls, seated rowing, and other low to moderate-intensity movements, which had negligible effects on the cardiovascular and vestibular systems.

sec.title: 2.5.2. Adherence and safety
sec.p: Attendance was carefully monitored. Adherence was 85% (IG) and 82% (CG). Adverse events were monitored throughout the 8-week intervention period. Research staff (including trainers and assessors) observed participants in real time during each training session. Safety monitoring was based on a predefined list of adverse events, which included, but was not limited to: any incident requiring session suspension; any incident requiring on-site first aid (e.g., application of ice for impact or sprain); any exercise-related discomfort or injury reported by the participant or a parent; and session interruption for any reason (including refusal to participate, behavioral issues, or physical discomfort). Additionally, a 48-hour post-session follow-up was conducted via phone call or parent questionnaire to monitor delayed-onset muscle soreness or any other postexercise discomfort. Any potential adverse event was required to be recorded immediately in the study log, including the time, type, severity, and handling measures of the event. During the entire intervention, no adverse events were reported in either the IG or the CG.

sec.title: 2.5.3. Outcome measures
sec.p: The primary outcomes included anxiety levels, measured via the SCARED questionnaire, and HRV. The secondary outcomes included BMI, lower explosive power (measured by standing long jump), and balance (measured by a one-leg stance with one’s eyes closed). Assessments were conducted at baseline and after the 8-week intervention.

sec.title: 2.5.3.1. Anxiety
sec.p: The Chinese version of the “Screening Tool for Anxiety Disorders in Children” (SCARED) revised by Chen Jie qiong (2012) was used to assess the anxiety levels of children.[21] The form was filled out by parents or caregivers. To mitigate potential expectation bias, parents or caregivers were informed that the study aimed to evaluate the benefits of 2 different types of physical activity programs for children with ASD, and that both interventions were expected to be beneficial. The scoring process strictly followed the procedures specified in the manual of this scale.

This study also selected HRV as a physiological indicator for assessing anxiety in children with ASD.[13] HRV can noninvasively and in real-time reflect the balance state of the autonomic nervous system,[25] and is particularly suitable for monitoring the anxiety changes in the ASD population.[11] HRV was recorded under standardized conditions to minimize potential confounders. All assessments were conducted in a quiet, temperature-controlled room (22–24°C) during the same time window (9:00–11:00 am) to control for diurnal variation.[10] Participants were instructed to refrain from caffeine intake for at least 6 hours. Measurements were taken after a 10-minute seated rest period to ensure stabilization of the autonomic nervous system. This report presents RMSSD as the primary HRV indicator.[12] Due to the limitations of the research design and equipment protocol, this study did not analyze frequency domain parameters (such as high frequency [HF] and low frequency [LF], or the LF/HF). While these parameters are well established in HRV methodology,[25] their absence does not affect the validity of our primary time-domain outcome (RMSSD), which is a reliable index of parasympathetic activity.

sec.title: 2.5.3.2. Standing long jump (cm; SLJ)
sec.p: Lower limb explosive power was tested through the standing long jump. The children to be tested stand slightly apart with both feet behind the take-off line and try to jump forward as far as possible.[2] The best result of 3 tests was recorded. The standing long jump was selected due to its minimal equipment requirements, simplicity, and high feasibility/acceptance in the present study population.[5] Future studies may incorporate more standardized instrumented measures (e.g., force plates or accelerometers) to derive precise kinetic parameters such as flight time and peak power.[22]

sec.title: 2.5.3.3. One-leg stance with eyes closed(s) (OLS)
sec.p: Static balance ability is evaluated by closed-eye single-leg standing.[23] The subjects need to stand on one leg, with the knee slightly bent, the arms naturally hanging down, close their eyes and try to maintain balance as much as possible. Testing was conducted on a flat, firm, nonslip surface with participants barefoot. The nonsupport leg was required to be lifted at least 15 cm off the ground. The stance leg (dominant or nondominant) was randomly assigned at the first assessment and kept consistent for the posttest. A researcher provided safety supervision but no balance assistance or feedback.[19] The best result of 3 trials was recorded, with adequate rest between trials to avoid fatigue.[23]

sec.title: 2.6. Data analysis
sec.p: Data were analyzed using SPSS 26.0. Shapiro–Wilk tests indicated non-normal distribution of all outcomes (all P < .05); thus, nonparametric tests were applied. Within-group comparisons were performed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and between-group differences (Δ-scores for IG vs CG) were assessed via the Mann–Whitney U test. Effect sizes were calculated as Cliff δ (d; thresholds: 0.11 = small, 0.28 = medium, 0.43 = large). All analyses adhered to the intention-to-treat principle. Due to the low dropout rate and absence of major adverse events, no data imputation was performed.

To assess the robustness of our findings, we additionally performed quantile regression (median regression) adjusting for age and gender as covariates. This approach allows for examination of intervention effects at the median of the outcome distribution while controlling for potential confounders, complementing the primary nonparametric analyses.

sec.title: 3.1. Participant flow and baseline characteristics
sec.p: A total of 50 children with mild-to-moderate ASD were assessed for eligibility, all of whom met the inclusion criteria and were enrolled in the study. Participants were randomly assigned to either the trampoline exercise IG (IG, n = 25) or the resistance training control group (CG, n = 25). All 50 participants completed the 8-week intervention and all post-intervention assessments, resulting in a 0% dropout rate and full data sets available for intention-to-treat analysis (Fig. 1). Baseline characteristics of the participants are presented in Table 2. The 2 groups were comparable at baseline with respect to age, gender distribution, ASD severity level, height and weight (all P > .05), indicating successful randomization.

sec.title: 3.2. Anxiety
sec.p: Compared with CG, IG showed significantly greater reductions in SCARED scores (Δ = −9.4 vs Δ = 0, P < .001, false discovery rate-corrected P < .001, δ = −0.92) and improvements in HRV (RMSSD: Δ = +9.76 ms vs Δ = +1.92 ms, P = .01, false discovery rate-corrected P = .003, δ = −0.66; Table 3).

sec.title: 3.3. Standing long jump (cm; SLJ)
sec.p: Standing long jump improved markedly in IG (Δ = +17.44 cm vs CG Δ = +4.2 cm, P < .001, false discovery rate-corrected P < .001, δ = −0.68; Table 3).

sec.title: 3.4. One-leg stance with eyes closed(s) (OLS)
sec.p: Stand with eyes closed showed no significant change after correction (Δ = −0.38 seconds vs CG Δ = +1.15 seconds, unadjusted P = .026, false discovery rate-corrected P = .076; Table 3).

sec.title: 3.5. Body mass index (BMI)
sec.p: BMI remained stable in both groups (P > .05; Table 3). BMI in IG decreased slightly (Median: 3.24→2.68, P = .05).

sec.title: 3.6. Within-group changes
sec.p: Detailed within-group pre-post comparisons for all outcomes are presented in Table 4. Briefly, both groups showed significant improvements in HRV and standing long jump performance after the 8-week intervention (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, false discovery rate-corrected P < .05). No statistically significant within-group changes were observed for SCARED scores, stand with eyes closed, or BMI in either group after false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons.

sec.title: 4. Discussion
sec.p: This randomized controlled trial demonstrates that an 8-week trampoline exercise program yields significant benefits for children with mild-to-moderate ASD, primarily by reducing anxiety and enhancing lower limb explosive power. Notably, these primary findings for anxiety (SCARED, HRV) and lower limb power (SLJ) remained statistically significant after applying false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons, underscoring the robustness of these intervention effects. In contrast, the intervention did not yield significant improvements in static balance or BMI.

The IG exhibited a substantial reduction in anxiety, as evidenced by a significant decrease in SCARED scores (Δ = −9.4) that far exceeds the established minimal clinically important difference for child anxiety scales.[32] This subjective improvement was corroborated by a physiologically objective measure, with a concurrent significant increase in HRV (RMSSD),[11] a key indicator of enhanced parasympathetic activity and reduced anxiety.[12,25] The concordance between these measures provides strong and multifaceted support for the anxiolytic effect of trampoline exercise in this population.[8] Given the high prevalence of anxiety disorders among children with ASD,[16] the identification of an accessible, non-pharmacological intervention is particularly valuable.[22]

A marked improvement was also observed in standing long jump performance, indicating enhanced lower limb explosive power.[5] The elastic surface of the trampoline is posited to play a crucial role in this enhancement, likely by promoting tendon energy storage and release during the stretch-shortening cycle.[17] Furthermore, the dynamic and repetitivenature of the jumping exercises may have contributed to improved neuromuscular coordination and motor planning, which are often areas of difficulty for children with ASD.[6] These findings align with previous research demonstrating that plyometric-style training can enhance lower-extremity performance adaptations.[29]

In contrast to these positive outcomes, the intervention did not yield significant improvements in static balance, as measured by the one-leg stance test with eyes closed.[19] This null finding may be attributed to the relatively short intervention period, as 8 weeks may be insufficient to induce the neuroplastic adaptations within the vestibular-cerebellar pathways that underpin static postural control.[17] Additionally, the inherent sensory challenges and potential intolerance to eye-closure tasks in some children with ASD could have limited measurable gains.[6] Similarly, no significant changes in BMI were observed in either group, a result consistent with previous short-term exercise studies and potentially explained by energy compensation effects, wherein increased appetite following exercise offsets caloric expenditure.[27]

From a mechanistic perspective, although not directly measured in this study, the observed benefits, particularly in anxiety reduction, invite consideration of potential underlying pathways.[11] The rhythmic vestibular stimulation inherent to trampoline exercise may enhance vagal tone via the nucleus tractus solitarius,[15] thereby promoting parasympathetic dominance and emotional regulation.[18] Furthermore, as a form of aerobic exercise, it may stimulate the release of β-endorphins, which are associated with mood improvement.[9] The combined vestibular-proprioceptive input could also help modulate sensory over-responsivity, a common feature in ASD that contributes to anxious behaviors.[14] Additionally, emerging evidence suggests that attentional disengagement deficits, which are linked to the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine system in children with ASD28, may be ameliorated by rhythmic physical activities like trampoline exercise, potentially contributing to reduced anxiety through improved attentional control. Recent advances in neuromodulation research suggest that interventions targeting autonomic regulation, such as transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation, may share common pathways with the effects observed in this study.[31] Future research should directly investigate these mechanisms by incorporating functional neuroimaging (e.g., functional magnetic resonance imaging) to examine changes in neural circuits, such as cerebellar-limbic connectivity, and by measuring biomarkers like salivary cortisol to quantify HPA axis activity.[10]

This study has several limitations. First, the primary subjective measure of anxiety (SCARED) relied on parent proxy-reports, which may not fully align with the child’s internal experience. Regarding HRV analysis, we reported only the time-domain parameter RMSSD. While RMSSD is a reliable index of parasympathetic activity and is widely used in anxiety research,[24] the absence of frequency-domain parameters (e.g., HF, LF/HF) limits a more comprehensive interpretation of autonomic nervous system balance.[25] Future studies are encouraged to incorporate multi-method assessments, such as child-friendly pictorial self-report scales (e.g., Spence Children’s Anxiety Scale) or biological markers like salivary cortisol.[10,28] Second, there are limitations regarding the assessment methods for secondary outcomes. Lower limb explosive power was measured solely via the standing long jump, which, while practical, does not provide fine-grained parameters of muscle mechanics (e.g., rate of concentric contraction).[22] Similarly, balance was assessed using the common clinical test of eyes-closed single-leg stance.[23] Although we standardized the testing surface, footwear condition, and lift height, the “best of 3 trials” protocol may introduce a learning effect, and the test’s challenge to the vestibular and proprioceptive systems may not be sufficiently sensitive to detect subtle intervention-induced changes.[17] Future investigations should combine instrumented assessments (e.g., force plates, center-of-pressure trajectory analysis) with more challenging dynamic balance tasks. Third, the sample size calculation was based on a small pilot study, which may have overestimated the effect size; however, the observed effects in this trial were large and clinically meaningful. Furthermore, although the active CG (resistance band training) was designed to control for the general effects of physical activity and to isolate the specific vestibular-aerobic component of the trampoline exercise, it did not fully match the IG for nonspecific factors such as the level of structured adult attention, social interaction, and the novelty of the exercise setting. These elements could have contributed to the observed reductions in anxiety, independent of the trampoline’s unique mechanisms. Therefore, we cannot definitively rule out the confounding effect of increased social engagement and attention on our primary outcome. The absence of a nonintervention CG precludes conclusions about absolute efficacy compared to no treatment, though the use of an active control strengthens the specificity of the findings to the trampoline modality. The lack of long-term follow-up means the durability of the benefits remains unknown. Future multicenter studies with larger samples are recommended to confirm and extend these findings. Importantly, future trials should consider incorporating an attention-CG that matches the experimental intervention in all nonspecific aspects (e.g., session duration, frequency, trainer contact, and social setting) while lacking the putative active component (vestibular-aerobic exercise), to more precisely isolate the therapeutic mechanisms of trampoline-based interventions.

Notwithstanding these limitations, the findings hold significant practical promise. Trampoline exercise is a low-cost (<$100/unit), safe, and highly adherent (85%) intervention that simultaneously addresses 2 critical domains in ASD – anxiety and motor proficiency. Its feasibility and dual benefits strongly support its potential integration into school-based programs or individualized education plans (IEPs). Given the documented disparities in ASD identification and intervention access across different populations, scalable interventions like trampoline exercise may help address existing gaps in service delivery. Future multicenter studies with extended follow-up periods are warranted to confirm these effects and explore the long-term implications.

sec.title: 5. Conclusion
sec.p: An 8-week trampoline exercise program (3 sessions/wk, 30 min/session) significantly reduces anxiety (via SCARED and HRV) and improves lower limb explosive power in children aged 9 to 14 years with mild-to-moderate ASD. With its low cost (<$100), high adherence (85%), and safety, trampoline exercise is a feasible adjunct to school-based or clinical interventions for ASD. Future multicenter studies with long-term follow-up are needed to confirm these effects.
